questions.stem: Thera (modern Santorini) lies in which island group of the Aegean Sea?
options: The Ionian Islands, west of the Peloponnese
The Sporades, north-east of the island of Euboea
The Cyclades, about 110 km north of Crete
The Dodecanese, just off the coast of Lycia
questions.explanation: Thera is the southernmost large island of the Cyclades, roughly 110 km north of Crete. This position placed it on sea routes between Crete, the other Cyclades and the Greek mainland.

questions.stem: The crescent shape of modern Santorini, around a deep flooded basin, is mainly the result of:
options: a large earthquake that split one island in two
the collapse of the volcano to form a caldera
a river delta slowly drowned by the rising sea
the erosion of soft limestone by Aegean storms
questions.explanation: Santorini's islands are the rim of a caldera, a basin formed when a volcano empties and collapses during huge eruptions. The Late Bronze Age eruption enlarged the caldera that already existed.

questions.stem: Why was Thera's location an advantage for a Bronze Age settlement such as Akrotiri?
options: It had wide, well-watered river plains ideal for growing grain
It controlled the narrow strait leading into the Black Sea
It lay on sea routes linking Crete, the Cyclades and the mainland
It was far from any other island, so it was safe from all contact
questions.explanation: Thera sat between Crete and the rest of the Aegean, so ships could stop there and its people could take part in trade. It had volcanic soils but no large rivers, and it is nowhere near the Black Sea straits.

questions.stem: During the period when Akrotiri flourished, the most powerful culture in the southern Aegean was:
options: the Classical Athenian empire, based on the Delian League
the Roman Republic, which ruled the islands from Italy
the Persian Empire, which governed the Aegean as a satrapy
the Minoan culture of Crete, with palaces such as Knossos
questions.explanation: Akrotiri's final phase belongs to the Late Bronze Age, when the Minoan palaces of Crete (the Neopalatial period) dominated the southern Aegean. Classical Athens, Rome and Persia came more than a thousand years later.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the wider Bronze Age world at the time of Akrotiri's final phase?
options: Mycenaean kings ruled Crete from Knossos, and the Hittite Empire had already been destroyed
Greek city-states had founded colonies across the western Mediterranean
Iron weapons had replaced bronze and the palaces had all been abandoned
Minoan palaces flourished, the Mycenaeans were rising, and Egypt traded across the sea
questions.explanation: In this period Crete's palaces were at their height, the Mycenaean mainland was growing in wealth (as the shaft graves at Mycenae show), and Egypt and the Near East were linked to the Aegean by trade. Mycenaean control of Knossos and the Iron Age came later.

questions.stem: Who began the systematic excavation of Akrotiri in 1967?
options: Arthur Evans
Heinrich Schliemann
Carl Blegen
Spyridon Marinatos
questions.explanation: The Greek archaeologist Spyridon Marinatos began excavating at Akrotiri in 1967. Arthur Evans excavated Knossos on Crete, and Schliemann and Blegen are linked with Troy and Mycenae.

questions.stem: Spyridon Marinatos argued in 1939, long before he dug at Akrotiri, that the Theran eruption:
options: had taken place in Roman times and buried only a small, poor fishing village
was a myth invented by Plato to explain the story of Atlantis
had no effect beyond the island because the wind blew the ash west
helped cause the destruction of Minoan Crete through ash and tsunamis
questions.explanation: Marinatos proposed that the eruption, with its tsunamis and ash, played a large part in the collapse of Minoan civilisation. His search for evidence led him to Akrotiri in the 1960s, although his theory is now widely rejected.

questions.stem: After Spyridon Marinatos died at the site in 1974, the excavation of Akrotiri was directed by:
options: Leonard Woolley
Amedeo Maiuri
Christos Doumas
Manfred Korfmann
questions.explanation: Christos Doumas, who had worked with Marinatos, led the excavation after his death and published widely on the site. Korfmann worked at Troy, Woolley at Ur and Maiuri at Herculaneum.

questions.stem: In the 1860s, before any planned excavation, ancient walls were found under the pumice of Thera when:
options: Arthur Evans sent a team from Knossos to search for Minoan palaces
an earthquake split open the cliffs and exposed painted rooms
Greek farmers dug wells and struck the roof of the West House
the pumice was quarried for building works such as the Suez Canal
questions.explanation: Quarrying of Theran pumice and ash for cement, used in works such as the Suez Canal, exposed Bronze Age walls, which the French geologist Ferdinand Fouque studied. Evans did not begin at Knossos until 1900.

questions.stem: Excavators at Akrotiri poured plaster into hollows left in the volcanic ash. What did this technique recover?
options: The shapes of wooden furniture such as beds and stools that had decayed
The bodies of the inhabitants who were trapped by the pyroclastic flows
The full contents of a royal archive written on wax-covered tablets
The original colours of wall paintings that had faded in the ash
questions.explanation: Wooden furniture rotted away but left its shape in the hardened ash, and plaster casts recovered beds, stools and tables. No bodies have been found at Akrotiri, so this was not used to cast victims.

questions.stem: A protective roof was built over the excavated part of Akrotiri. What problem was it mainly meant to solve?
options: Looters were removing frescoes from the site during the night
The roof was needed to hold up the ash that still covered the town
Tourists had to be kept away from the buildings altogether
Exposed walls and floors were being damaged by sun, rain and wind
questions.explanation: Once uncovered, the mud-brick, timber and stone remains began to deteriorate, so a roof was built to shelter them. Part of the roof collapsed in 2005, closing the site for several years while a new one was built.

questions.stem: The Spring Fresco from Akrotiri shows:
options: a fleet of ships sailing between harbour towns
two young boys boxing, one wearing a single glove
young girls gathering crocus flowers to offer to a goddess
red lilies on rocky hills with swallows flying between them
questions.explanation: The Spring Fresco covers three walls of a room with lilies and swallows in a rocky landscape, with no people. The ships, boxers and crocus gatherers are other Akrotiri paintings.

questions.stem: Most of Akrotiri's wall paintings were made by applying pigment to wet lime plaster. Why does this matter for historians?
options: The paint dissolved in the ash, so all colours are modern restorations
The method was used only in Egypt, proving Egyptian artists made them
It shows the paintings were added long after the town was destroyed
The colours bonded with the plaster, so many paintings survive vividly
questions.explanation: In painting on wet plaster (fresco), the pigment binds as the plaster sets, so many Akrotiri paintings kept their colours under the ash. Restorers have reassembled fragments, but the colours are largely original.

questions.stem: The Young Boxers fresco shows two boys with mostly shaved heads and a few long locks. Many scholars interpret the hairstyles as:
options: an error by an artist who never finished the painting
a sign of age, marking stages in a young person's life
proof that the two boys were enslaved captives from Egypt
a sign that both boys were priests of a sea god
questions.explanation: Across Akrotiri's paintings, young people have partly shaved heads with locks, and hair grows longer with age, so hairstyle is read as a marker of age. Nothing in the image identifies the boys as captives or priests.

questions.stem: The Fisherman frescoes from the West House show young men carrying strings of fish. Which conclusion do they best support?
options: Akrotiri imported all of its food because the island had no fish nearby
Fishermen were the ruling class who governed the island
Fishing was done only by women, since men were all sailors
Fishing mattered to Akrotiri, and fish may have been offerings or food
questions.explanation: The paintings show the importance of the sea's catch, and some scholars see the fish as offerings, which fits the religious use of some rooms. Nothing in them shows that fishermen ruled the town.

questions.stem: The miniature Naval Campaign (Flotilla) fresco in the West House shows decorated ships moving between towns and, in one scene, warriors with boar's tusk helmets. Why is this scene debated?
options: Boar's tusk helmets are linked with the Mycenaeans, so it may show mainland contact
It shows Roman warships, which proves the fresco was painted many centuries later
The ships are Egyptian, which proves Egypt ruled Thera at the time
It is the only painting at Akrotiri that shows any people at all
questions.explanation: Boar's tusk helmets are best known from Mycenaean Greece, so the scene raises questions about contact or conflict with the mainland. Interpretations range from a real expedition to a festival or a mythic story.

questions.stem: A historian claims that the Naval Campaign fresco is a reliable record of a particular sea battle. Which response is strongest?
options: The claim is correct, since all Aegean art was strictly documentary in purpose
The claim is wrong, since the fresco was painted in Classical times
The scene may be ceremonial or idealised, and no text names any event
The claim is correct, since a Linear B caption names the admiral
questions.explanation: No inscription accompanies the fresco, and the festive ships and towns could show a celebration or an ideal view, so it cannot simply be read as a record of a battle. It is Bronze Age, not Classical.

questions.stem: Paintings in Xeste 3 show young women gathering crocus flowers and offering saffron to a seated female figure flanked by a griffin and a monkey. The seated figure is usually interpreted as:
options: a goddess receiving offerings in a religious ceremony
a merchant buying saffron to export to the mainland
a queen of Crete visiting the island to collect taxes
an Egyptian princess given in marriage to a Theran ruler
questions.explanation: The griffin and monkey, and her raised position, suggest a deity, and the scene is often read as a ritual, perhaps an initiation of girls. Saffron also had value as a dye and medicine, but the scene's focus is religious.

questions.stem: Which feature of Akrotiri's buildings shows a high level of town planning?
options: A single great palace with a throne room at its centre
Broad avenues laid out on a strict grid like Roman towns
Fortification walls with towers around the whole town
Paved streets with drains running beneath them
questions.explanation: Akrotiri had paved streets with drains below, and some houses had toilets connected to them. No palace has been found, the streets are irregular, and the town has no known defensive wall.

questions.stem: Buildings at Akrotiri were often two or three storeys high and built with timber framing in the walls. The timber most likely helped to:
options: keep the buildings cool by letting air through the walls
hide the rooms used for storage from tax collectors
carry rainwater from the roof down to the drains under the street
make the walls more flexible and resistant to earthquakes
questions.explanation: Timber set into stone and mud-brick walls gave them flexibility, a sensible response to frequent earthquakes. Evidence shows the town had already been damaged by earthquakes and was being repaired before the eruption.

questions.stem: Xeste 3 is built of finely cut stone blocks and has a sunken 'lustral basin' and many wall paintings. Archaeologists use these features to argue that it was:
options: a barracks for Minoan soldiers stationed on the island
an ordinary family house with no special use beyond living in
a public building with a religious or ceremonial purpose
a granary run by the state to feed the whole town
questions.explanation: Ashlar masonry, a lustral basin like those at Cretan palaces and the saffron paintings point to ritual use. There is no sign that it was a barracks or granary.

questions.stem: Large clay storage jars (pithoi) found at Akrotiri held remains such as grain, pulses and oil. This evidence best shows that:
options: households stored surplus food and goods, some perhaps for trade
the town depended entirely on food sent each year as tribute from Egypt
the inhabitants did not farm, but lived entirely by fishing
the jars were placed in tombs as gifts for the dead
questions.explanation: Stored produce points to farming, surplus and possibly exchange. The jars were found in buildings, not graves, and fishing was only one part of the economy.

questions.stem: Pottery found at Akrotiri includes local Cycladic wares and vessels imported from Crete and the mainland. For historians, this mix is useful mainly because it:
options: proves that the island was ruled directly by Knossos
shows that the islanders could not make their own pots
provides written records of every transaction in the town
helps date the layers and shows the town's trading links
questions.explanation: Imported pottery shows contact with other places, and known pottery styles help date the deposits relative to Crete and the mainland. Local wares show that Therans made their own pottery, and pots alone do not prove political control.

questions.stem: No human bodies and very few valuable objects have been found at Akrotiri. What is the most widely accepted explanation?
options: The town had been abandoned for centuries before the eruption
Roman treasure hunters removed the bodies and the valuables
Earthquakes warned the people, who left before the main eruption
The inhabitants were all killed and their bodies burnt by the lava
questions.explanation: Signs of earthquake damage, repair work and cleared rooms suggest the population left in time, taking valuables with them. Whether they survived the eruption elsewhere is unknown.

questions.stem: Compared with Pompeii, why does Akrotiri give less evidence about individual people?
options: The ash at Akrotiri destroyed every building down to the foundations
Akrotiri was excavated in the 1700s with no records kept
The town was much smaller than a single house at Pompeii
No bodies, tombs with names or long inscriptions have been found
questions.explanation: At Akrotiri there are no victims, no surviving written texts beyond a few Linear A marks, and few graves, so people are known only through buildings, objects and paintings. The buildings survive well, some to more than one storey.

questions.stem: Which of these activities is supported by evidence from Akrotiri?
options: Glass-blowing in workshops on the main square
Weaving, shown by many loom weights found in the houses
Iron smelting in large furnaces outside the town
Coin minting for use in trade with the other Cyclades
questions.explanation: Loom weights show that textiles were made in houses. Coinage, iron working and glass-blowing all belong to much later periods.

questions.stem: Historians debate whether Akrotiri was mainly a trading port or a religious centre. Which evidence best supports the trading interpretation?
options: Imported goods, Minoan-style weights and the ships in the West House paintings
The lustral basin in Xeste 3 and the paintings of a goddess seated on a platform
The absence of bodies and valuables from the excavated buildings
The plaster casts of beds and stools found in many houses
questions.explanation: Foreign pottery, weights for measuring goods and depictions of ships point to trade. The lustral basin and goddess support the religious view, and the missing bodies concern the evacuation.

questions.stem: Which is the most defensible judgement about Akrotiri's role?
options: It was a prosperous port town in which religion was also important
It was a purely religious sanctuary with no permanent population at all
It was a fortress built only to defend Crete from the mainland
It was a poor fishing village with no contact beyond the island
questions.explanation: The evidence of trade, workshops, storage and rich houses sits alongside clear religious buildings and imagery, so most historians see both roles. There is no fortress, and the wealth of the town rules out a poor isolated village.

questions.stem: Which evidence shows strong Minoan influence at Akrotiri?
options: Linear B tablets recording the tribute paid each year to Mycenae
Greek temples with columns built in the Doric order
Cuneiform letters sent from the king of Babylon
Linear A signs, Minoan-style frescoes and a lustral basin
questions.explanation: Linear A, lustral basins, Minoan weights and painting styles all show close links with Crete. Linear B was used later by Mycenaean Greeks, and Doric temples belong to the Archaic and Classical periods.

questions.stem: Some scholars describe Akrotiri as 'Minoanised' rather than a Minoan colony. This view is based mainly on the point that:
options: Linear A was invented on Thera and later borrowed by Crete
Theran art and pottery adopted Cretan styles but kept local features
No object made on Crete has ever been found anywhere on the island of Thera
Akrotiri was founded only after the Minoan palaces were destroyed
questions.explanation: Akrotiri took up much from Crete, but its paintings, pottery and houses have distinctive Cycladic features, which suggests strong cultural influence without proving direct rule. Cretan objects are in fact found on Thera.

questions.stem: Why is the date of the Theran eruption so important to Aegean archaeologists?
options: A layer of its ash is a time marker for sites across the region
It is the only date in Greek history recorded on a coin
It marks the exact year in which Plato recorded the fall of Atlantis
It was written down by Egyptian scribes who saw it happen
questions.explanation: Theran ash found on Crete, other islands and the coast of Anatolia provides a shared marker for dating Bronze Age layers. No contemporary text records the eruption.

questions.stem: Radiocarbon dating, including an olive branch buried by the eruption, has suggested a date in the late 1600s BCE, while many archaeologists have preferred a date near 1500 BCE. The archaeologists' date was based mainly on:
options: the number of years recorded in the Linear A tablets of Akrotiri
the age of the plaster casts measured by tree-ring counting
Greek writers who gave the exact year of the eruption
links between Aegean pottery styles and dated Egyptian contexts
questions.explanation: The traditional date comes from cross-dating Aegean pottery found with Egyptian material whose reign dates are known. Scientific methods have tended to give earlier results, and the debate remains open, so the date is usually given as a range.

questions.stem: Which effect of the eruption on the wider Aegean is supported by geological evidence?
options: The immediate destruction of every Minoan palace on Crete on the very same day
The sinking of the whole Greek mainland below the sea
A lava flow that crossed the sea and reached Knossos
Ash falls on Crete and other areas, and tsunami deposits on Crete's coast
questions.explanation: Ash layers have been found in Crete, the eastern Aegean and Anatolia, and deposits on Crete's north coast point to tsunamis. Lava does not cross open sea, and the palaces were not all destroyed at once.

questions.stem: Excavations on Crete show that Minoan palaces were still in use for some time after the Theran ash fell. How does this affect Marinatos's theory?
options: It shows the eruption had no effect at all on any part of Crete
It confirms that tsunamis destroyed Knossos within a single day
It weakens the idea that the eruption alone caused the Minoan collapse
It proves the eruption happened long after the Minoan palaces had all fallen
questions.explanation: If palaces continued after the eruption, it cannot have been the immediate cause of their fall, though it may have weakened Minoan society. Many historians now stress later factors such as Mycenaean takeover.

questions.stem: The story of Atlantis, which some writers link with Thera, comes from:
options: Plato's dialogues Timaeus and Critias
Homer's account of Odysseus's travels
Herodotus's history of the Persian Wars
Linear A tablets found in Xeste 3
questions.explanation: Plato told of Atlantis, a powerful island sunk in a day and a night. Some modern writers connect it with Thera's eruption, but Plato wrote over a thousand years later and his story may be a moral fable.

questions.stem: A television documentary presents Thera as 'the real Atlantis'. How should a historian treat this representation?
options: As a popular theory resting on later myth, not on Bronze Age evidence
As proven fact, since Plato named Thera as Atlantis in his account of the island
As a reliable account written by the Akrotiri excavators
As false, since Thera was never hit by any eruption
questions.explanation: Plato does not name Thera, and his Atlantis story differs in size, place and date, so the link is speculative. The eruption itself is certain, but Atlantis is a later representation shaped by myth.

questions.stem: The West House is sometimes called the house of an admiral or ship's captain because of its ship paintings. What is the main weakness of this interpretation?
options: Excavators found the owner's name painted above the door in Greek
The house contained no paintings of ships, sailors or of the sea at all
It was a temple, as a Linear B inscription in it proves
No written evidence names its owner, so it rests on reading the art
questions.explanation: The 'admiral' label is a modern inference from the subject of the paintings. Without texts, the owner and his role cannot be known, so this is an interpretation rather than a fact.
